D.treatment: structured interprofessional simulation-enhanced training with debriefing

O.outcome_detail: self-reported realization of workplace commitments to change

result.effect: 57 of 62 commitments (91.9%) at least partly realized

cells.quote: At the two months follow-up (t2), 32 participants (50%) provided written comments on their original commitments. At follow-up, 57 of the 62 (91.9%) commitments were reported to be at least partly realized, and only five (8.1%) commitments (still) lacked realization.
cells.note: Single-group follow-up with no concurrent comparison; realization was self-reported.

cells.quote: We did not observe any significant correlations between the strength of commitments and the probability of their realization (r=0.222; p=0.1), suggesting that realization is more strongly influenced by external factors in the workplace than by participant motivation.
cells.note: This is an observed association, not a randomized contrast.

cells.quote: The best rate of commitment realization was (self-) reported by trainees of emergency nursing, with 13 fully implemented commitments out of 31 (41.9%).
cells.note: Descriptive subgroup comparison; no inferential test or adjustment is reported, and implementation was self-reported.

O.outcome_detail: age difference between responder and non-responder groups

cells.quote: There were no significant differences between groups in age (p = 0.340) and gender (p = 0.294).
cells.note: The study reports a non-significant age difference without an equivalence test or adequate-power claim.

O.outcome_detail: gender difference between responder and non-responder groups

cells.quote: There were no significant differences between groups in age (p = 0.340) and gender (p = 0.294).
cells.note: The study reports a non-significant gender difference without an equivalence test or adequate-power claim.

D.treatment: emergency nursing trainees and student paramedics

cells.quote: However, trainees of emergency nursing (n=14; 77.8% response rate on follow-up) and student paramedics (n=13; 59.1%) were significantly more likely to respond than medical students (n=1; 6.7%; p < 0.01; Pearson’s chi-squared test).
cells.note: This is an exploratory nonresponse-bias comparison by profession after 50% dropout between initial assessment and follow-up.

result.effect: 64 of 90 participants (71.1%) made at least one commitment; 123 commitments

cells.quote: In total, 64 of 90 participants (71.1%) made at least one commitment to change after the training modules.
cells.note: Single-group descriptive outcome; no comparison condition was reported. The abstract reports 64 of 80 participants, whereas the full-text Impact/Effectiveness section reports 64 of 90.

result.effect: 57 of 62 commitments (91.9%) at least partly realized; 5 (8.1%) not realized

cells.quote: At follow-up, 57 of the 62 (91.9%) commitments were reported to be at least partly realized, and only five (8.1%) commitments (still) lacked realization.
cells.note: Self-reported follow-up with 50% participant response; no control or baseline comparison was reported.

cells.quote: We did not observe any significant correlations between the strength of commitments and the probability of their realization (r=0.222; p=0.1), suggesting that realization is more strongly influenced by external factors in the workplace than by participant motivation.
cells.note: This is a measured association rather than a treatment comparison; the nonsignificant result is coded ns because no power or equivalence test was reported.

cells.quote: Textual data, such as commitments, or responses regarding factors that fostered or hindered implementation of the intended changes, were inductively categorized by three researchers (DE, FS, and JG) according to Mayring.
cells.note: Qualitative inductive categorization with consensus coding and independent psychologist consistency checking; no comparison condition was reported.
